Chapter 1: Creativity Belongs to Everyone, Not Just a Chosen Few
You know, there’s this quiet longing inside so many of us—a gentle urge to make something, to express a side of ourselves that rarely gets seen, or to bring a brand new idea into the world.
But all too often, that spark gets snuffed out by a voice telling us creativity is only for the gifted, the quirky, or just the lucky few.
Here’s the real truth, though—creativity isn’t a privilege for the chosen. It’s actually a birthright. It’s part of what it means to be human, woven right into who we are, just waiting for us to pay attention and say “yes.”
This kind of realization usually sneaks up on us in the smallest moments. Imagine someone who, after years of the same routine, finds themselves doodling in the margins of a notepad during a boring meeting. Maybe those little sketches don’t add up to much, but there’s a flicker of satisfaction that comes from simply letting the pen wander. Or think about humming a tune while you’re washing dishes—the melody briefly carries you away from the daily grind.
These aren’t dramatic, spotlight moments. But they are acts of creativity—tiny reminders that the urge to make and play is alive in everyone, no matter your age, background, or job.
Most of us grew up hearing that creativity is some rare superpower—something you either have or you don’t. Schools and society often reinforce this, giving gold stars only to the most obviously talented or productive.
But here’s something to pay attention to: creativity isn’t really about talent. It’s about willingness. It’s about showing up, staying curious, and daring to try—even when you have no idea how things will turn out.
Let me tell you about a woman who, after years focused on her family and work, felt this persistent itch to do something different. She remembered how much joy ice skating brought her as a kid. So, she bought a pair of skates and started visiting the local rink before work. She wasn’t chasing medals or applause—she just wanted to feel the ice glide beneath her feet again. In those quiet, early mornings, she rediscovered a playful sense of possibility she hadn’t felt in years.
Her story isn’t about being the best or getting recognition—it’s simply about reclaiming the joy of making something, just for herself.
The thing is, most people don’t realize that creativity doesn’t demand perfection—or even public praise. It only asks that you show up and participate. Whether you’re painting, writing a poem, planting a garden, or trying a new recipe, what matters most is the act of making itself. That process is a kind of conversation with the world—a way of saying, “I’m here, and I have something to share.”
This way of seeing things changes everything. Suddenly, creativity isn’t a contest or an exam. It becomes a conversation—an ongoing exchange between you and the world around you. And the more you lean into this process, the more natural it starts to feel.
Eventually, the line between “creative people” and “everyone else” just fades away, uncovering a simple, beautiful truth: everyone is creative. And everyone is welcome to join in.
